nature-eecon-202.title: Population growth: from one billion to eight
nature-eecon-202.text:
In 1800 the world held 1 billion people. By 2026 it held 8.3 billion, and it still adds about 70 million people, or 0.84%, every year. Population growth is simply the increase in the number of people in a {{ref:nature-eco-374}}.

Better farming, sanitation and medicine drove the rise. The global growth rate peaked at 2.2% a year in 1963 and has fallen ever since. In rich countries the demographic transition, the shift to smaller families, has slowed growth sharply.

Where it ends is uncertain. As of 2024 the UN projects a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s. The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation expects an earlier peak, 9.73 billion in 2064, falling to 8.89 billion by 2100.

The environmental stakes are high. Together with rising consumption, population growth drives biodiversity loss and climate change through overuse of natural resources. Reducing population is discussed as a sustainability strategy, but respect for free life choices limits what it can achieve.

nature-eecon-204.title: The Solow–Swan model: where long-run growth comes from
nature-eecon-204.text:
In 1956 Robert Solow and Trevor Swan, working independently, built a model that still anchors textbooks of long-run growth. Solow won the Nobel Prize in Economics for it in 1987.

The model allows output to grow in only three ways: more capital, a larger population, or technology that raises total factor productivity. Its key assumption is diminishing returns to capital. Each extra machine adds less output than the one before. So saving and investing more cannot keep growth going forever. Without technological progress, growth stops once new investment only replaces worn-out capital, the {{ref:nature-econ-519}}.

The striking conclusion follows. In the long run, lasting growth in income per person comes only from technological progress. Higher saving or faster population growth change only the level of income, not its growth rate. Yet the model does not explain why technology improves. It takes progress as given from outside, which is why it is called an exogenous growth model.

It also predicts that poor countries, with little capital, should grow faster and catch up with rich ones. Capital should flow towards them. That is seldom seen, a puzzle known as Lucas' paradox.

nature-eecon-203.title: Logistic growth: populations that level off
nature-eecon-203.text: Most populations of non-human species do not grow exponentially forever. They follow a logistic path: growth slows as the population nears its {{ref:nature-eco-593}}, the largest population its environment can sustain. At that point the curve levels off, usually when the population has used up most of its natural resources. Humans are different so far. Over the last few decades, human population growth has followed a roughly linear trend.

nature-eecon-201.title: The Golden Rule savings rate
nature-eecon-201.text: Save 100% of income and nothing is left to consume. Save 0% and capital wears out. The best rate lies in between: the Golden Rule savings rate, which gives the highest consumption per person that can be kept up forever in the {{ref:nature-eecon-204}}. Edmund Phelps named it in 1961, applying "do unto others" between generations. It is reached where the marginal product of capital equals population growth plus depreciation. An economy saving more is dynamically inefficient: it could consume more both now and later by saving less.

nature-eecon-206.title: The Mankiw–Romer–Weil model: adding education
nature-eecon-206.text: In 1992 a new version of the {{ref:nature-eecon-204}} added {{ref:nature-econ-531}}, such as education, as a factor of production. In this view poor countries have lower output and lower returns to capital because they have less human capital. The estimated model explained 78% of the variation in income across countries. Adding human capital also shrinks the part of growth left unexplained, the total factor productivity residual.

nature-eecon-207.title: Conditional convergence: catching up, with conditions
nature-eecon-207.text: The growth models predict that poor countries will catch up with rich ones, if they save similar shares of output in physical and human capital. Since the 1950s, output per worker in rich and poor countries has generally not converged. But poor countries that raised their saving rates have. Japan caught up after raising its saving rates in the 1950s and 1960s. Endogenous growth theories are criticized for failing to explain this conditional convergence in the data.

nature-eecon-205.title: The Solow residual: the growth nobody can account for
nature-eecon-205.text: Add up the growth that comes from more capital and labor, and something is left over. That leftover is the Solow residual, taken as a measure of {{ref:nature-econ-599}} growth. It is often credited entirely to technological progress, but it also includes lasting gains in how efficiently inputs are combined. Economists use Solow's growth accounting to separate the effects of technology, capital and labor on growth.

nature-eecon-200.title: The AK model: growth without diminishing returns
nature-eecon-200.text: The AK model is the simplest endogenous growth model: output is a straight-line function of capital, Y = AK. Here K covers both physical and human capital, and A is a constant level of technology. Its key feature is that capital has no diminishing returns, so growth need not fade to zero as in the {{ref:nature-eecon-204}}. Formally, it is a Cobb–Douglas function where the output elasticity of capital equals 1. Textbooks mostly use it to introduce {{ref:nature-econ-551}}.

nature-eecon-185.title: Overconsumption: using up faster than nature refills
nature-eecon-185.text:
By 1983 China's consumption had already surpassed the biocapacity of its natural resources. Growing economies can drive overconsumption: using goods, services or natural resources faster than they can be replenished or reused. Applied to natural resources harmed by use, it means the same as {{ref:nature-eco-063}}.

The drivers are partly built into how business works. Consumerism, {{ref:nature-eecon-188}}, economic materialism and other unsustainable business models push consumption up. It stands in contrast to {{ref:nature-eecon-196}}.

Over the long term, overconsumption in a region shrinks natural resources and degrades the environment. Consuming beyond the environment's long-term {{ref:nature-eco-593}} causes {{ref:nature-eecon-173}}, resource depletion and poorer ecosystem health. In 2010 the International Resource Panel found that household consumption for mobility, shelter, food and energy-using products causes most of the life-cycle impacts of consumption.

Movements push back: anti-consumerism, {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}, frugality, downshifting, simple living and minimalism. Many of them aim at a {{ref:nature-eecon-072}}. Even so, the term itself is controversial and lacks a single agreed definition.

nature-eecon-180.title: Human overpopulation: too many people, or too much consumption?
nature-eecon-180.text:
In 1804 the world held 1 billion people. Today it holds 8 billion, thanks to medical advances and higher farm productivity. The worry about human overpopulation is that populations may grow too large for their environment or resources to support over the long term.

The worry is old. In the early 19th century Thomas Malthus predicted that population would outgrow the resources a finite amount of land can supply. Today's proponents say that too many people, population growth and overconsumption together are the main drivers of human-caused problems such as climate change. The IPCC found that GDP per person and population growth were the strongest drivers of fossil CO2 emissions in 2010–2019. They raised emissions about 2.3% and 1.2% a year respectively.

The counter-evidence is substantial. Annual population growth peaked at 2.1% in 1968 and has dropped to 1.1%; the UN projects a peak of about 10.4 billion in the 2080s. Over 200 years of growth, poverty and infant mortality have declined, and the predicted "population explosion" never came. Critics also call the concept racist, because population control often targets the Global South rather than overconsumption in the Global North. Whether sheer numbers are a real cause of environmental problems, rather than consumption or technology, is strongly disputed.

nature-eecon-154.title: The Limits to Growth: a computer model meets a finite planet
nature-eecon-154.text:
On 2 March 1972 the {{ref:nature-hist-026}} published a report that put a simple question to a computer. What happens when the economy and population grow exponentially on a planet with finite resources? The authors were {{ref:nature-hist-059}}, {{ref:nature-hist-058}}, Jørgen Randers and William Behrens III, writing for a team of 17 researchers. They used the {{ref:nature-eecon-198}} model, built on Jay Forrester's work at MIT, to simulate how Earth and human systems interact.

The answer was stark. Two scenarios showed "overshoot and collapse" of the global system by the mid to late 21st century. If growth trends continued unchanged, limits would be reached within a hundred years, most likely with a sudden decline in population and industrial capacity. A third scenario produced a "stabilized world": a stable, sustainable equilibrium was possible.

The book sold about 30 million copies in 30 languages and influenced environmental reforms for decades. Updates followed in 1992 (Beyond the Limits), 2004 (the 30-Year Update) and 2022 (Limits and Beyond).

It was also fiercely attacked. Critics called it "Garbage In, Garbage Out", too simplistic and too pessimistic about technological progress, and its scarcity-based price predictions did not come true. Yet later comparisons with real data have found the world tracking its business-as-usual run. The argument is not settled.

nature-eecon-159.title: The rebound effect: when efficiency eats its own savings
nature-eecon-159.text:
Make a car 5% more fuel-efficient and you might expect fuel use to fall by 5%. If it falls by only 2%, the rebound is 60%. The rebound effect is the loss of part of the expected savings from a more efficient technology, because people and the economy respond by using more. The "missing" saving may go into driving faster or further than before.

{{ref:nature-hist-077}} first described it in his 1865 book The Coal Question. He observed that a more efficient steam engine opened many new uses for coal; in its extreme form this is the {{ref:nature-eecon-163}}. Though studied mostly for energy, the idea applies to any natural resource or input, labor included.

How big is it? Studies of home heating, cooling and personal transport often find rebounds of 20–50%. Direct rebounds tend to be higher in low-income households, which have been cutting back on heating because of its cost. A more efficient heater lets them finally keep warm.

Most economists agree the rebound effect exists. They disagree about how large it is and how much it matters for policy.

nature-eecon-183.title: I = PAT: impact as population times affluence times technology
nature-eecon-183.text:
In 1970 a public argument produced one of environmentalism's best-known formulas. Barry Commoner blamed production technology for environmental damage. Paul Ehrlich and John Holdren stressed population growth. Out of their debate came I = PAT: human impact (I) is the product of population (P), affluence (A) and technology (T).

Each term has a measure. Affluence is average consumption per person, often proxied by GDP per person. Technology measures how resource-intensive that affluence is, such as emissions per unit of GDP. Impact can be measured in global hectares with ecological footprint analysis. If impact exceeds carrying capacity, the system is in overshoot. The Kaya identity applies the same logic to carbon dioxide emissions, and I = PAT underpins the {{ref:nature-eecon-198}} simulation model.

Its simplicity is also its weakness. Critics say P, A and T are not independent. Halving T may not halve impact if cheaper use stimulates more consumption, the {{ref:nature-eecon-159}}. The formula is also faulted for ignoring political context and for blaming the global poor. Environmentalists still debate whether impact can be written as a simple product, and which factors matter most.

nature-eecon-147.title: Eco-economic decoupling: growth without more damage
nature-eecon-147.text:
In many economies, rising production increases pressure on the environment. Eco-economic decoupling is the idea that an economy could keep growing while using less water, fossil fuel and other resources. In 2002 the OECD defined it as breaking the link between "environmental bads" and "economic goods". It is often measured by emission intensity, the pollution per unit of GDP.

Where decoupling has occurred, one proposed explanation is the shift to a service economy, and the {{ref:nature-eecon-165}} is a proposed model of it. Proposed technologies to speed it include energy-saving, metal- and mineral-saving, and freshwater- and biotic-resource-saving ones.

The stakes are large. In 2011 the UNEP International Resource Panel issued a warning. Without decoupling, humanity could use 140 billion tons of minerals, ores, fossil fuels and biomass a year by 2050, three times the rate of that time. Its 2016 report brought bad news: global material productivity had declined since about 2000. The world economy needed more materials per unit of GDP, the opposite sometimes called overcoupling.

Whether, how far and how fast growth can be decoupled from environmental pressure is widely debated.

nature-eecon-143.title: Degrowth: shrinking production on purpose
nature-eecon-143.text:
The movement takes its name from French. Décroissance was the term used for a 1979 translation of essays by {{ref:nature-hist-044}}, whom degrowth names as its main intellectual inspiration. The first international degrowth conference met in Paris in 2008.

Degrowth is an academic and social movement, mainly in Europe, that calls for a planned, democratic reduction of production and consumption to tackle social and ecological crises. It rejects GDP growth as a measure of human and economic development. Capitalism's focus on growth, it argues, causes wide ecological damage and is not needed to raise living standards. Its common goals are to shrink humanity's environmental impact, redistribute income and wealth within and between countries, and move from materialistic values to a convivial, participatory society.

Degrowth writers doubt the alternative. Absolute {{ref:nature-eecon-147}} of GDP from resource use and emissions, they argue, is possible only briefly, in specific places, or with small cuts. Efficiency technologies can also trigger the {{ref:nature-eecon-159}}, cancelling out expected savings.

Critics call degrowth vague and politically unpopular, say it ignores rebound effects itself, and argue that environmental taxes or tradable permits work much better. Far-reaching degrowth scenarios are also projected to raise extreme poverty. Supporters reply that it would improve living standards and protect ecosystems. The dispute is open.

nature-eecon-152.title: Green growth: betting on decoupling
nature-eecon-152.text:
Green growth is the bet that economies can keep growing while harms such as climate change fall. The term means environmentally sustainable paths of economic growth. It depends on {{ref:nature-eecon-147}} from resource use and environmental impact.

Rae Kwon Chung of UNESCAP coined the term in 2005, and it first emerged at a ministerial conference in Seoul. The OECD published a Green Growth Strategy in 2011. In 2012 the World Bank, UNEP, OECD and GGGI launched the Green Growth Knowledge Platform. The ILO estimates a greener economy could create 24 million new jobs worldwide by 2030, if environmental policies are in place.

The evidence cuts both ways. One analysis found 92% of global GDP is in economies that have decoupled relatively or absolutely. Countries with over 46% of global GDP achieved absolute decoupling between 2015 and 2023. But claims based on domestic material consumption ignore resource use shifted along global supply chains. The material footprint, which counts it, suggests resource use may grow about as fast as GDP. A 2020 review of 835 papers concluded that observed decoupling cannot deliver large, rapid absolute cuts on its own. It needs sufficiency strategies and strict reduction targets alongside it. Researchers still disagree on whether green growth can meet environmental targets.

nature-eecon-191.title: Resource efficiency: the same output from less
nature-eecon-191.text: Resource efficiency means getting the same output or consumption from fewer of Earth's limited resources, with less environmental impact. Gains can come at a product's production, consumption and end-of-life stages. Its aims closely resemble those of {{ref:nature-eecon-193}}, {{ref:nature-eecon-192}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-027}}. A key tool is measuring resource use with carbon, water and land footprints, then finding the "hot spots" where most is used or most can be saved. A resource-efficient Europe was one of seven flagship initiatives of the EU's Europe 2020 strategy. The European Commission noted trade-offs: green vehicles cut fossil fuel use but add pressure on electricity, rare-earth elements and lithium.

nature-eecon-196.title: Sustainable consumption: buying and using with less harm
nature-eecon-196.text: The top 10% of people by income consume 56% of vehicle fuel, while the bottom half causes under 20% of energy footprints. Sustainable consumption means using products and services in ways that keep their environmental harm as small as possible. It covers the whole cycle: choosing, using and disposing of products. It includes buying sustainable products, avoiding unsustainable ones, and making products last through reuse and recycling. Diet matters, because food systems cause about one third of global human-made greenhouse gas emissions. The 1992 {{ref:nature-hist-003}} recognized the concept in chapter 4 of {{ref:nature-gov-127}}, and UN Sustainable Development Goal 12 aims to "ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns". Studies find that systemic change, not just individual ethical choices, is needed for a large effect on global warming.

nature-eecon-164.title: The Kuznets curve: does inequality rise and then fall?
nature-eecon-164.text: Simon Kuznets proposed that as an economy develops, market forces first raise and then lower economic inequality, tracing an inverted U. One explanation: early industrialization draws cheap rural labor to cities, holding wages down while owners profit. Later, democratization and the welfare state spread the gains. Kuznets himself warned that his data were fragile and covered a very limited period, but other economists raised the curve "to the level of law". The data have not been kind. Inequality has risen in most developed countries since the 1960s. The East Asian miracle, rapid growth with falling poverty in eight East Asian economies between 1965 and 1990, has also been used to challenge it. Economists have no consensus that the curve is real.

nature-eecon-146.title: Doughnut economics: a safe and just space for humanity
nature-eecon-146.text: Picture a doughnut. The hole in the middle holds people lacking life's essentials, such as healthcare and education. The outer crust marks ecological ceilings that must not be overshot. Between them lies a "safe and just space for humanity". Economist {{ref:nature-hist-042}} developed the image in a 2012 Oxfam paper and expanded it in her 2017 book Doughnut Economics. An economy counts as prosperous when it meets all twelve social foundations, drawn from the UN {{ref:nature-gov-010}}. It must do so without overshooting any of the nine ceilings from the {{ref:nature-eco-597}}. A 2018 study of 150 countries found none that met basic needs at a globally sustainable level of resource use. Raworth says low- and middle-income countries still need significant GDP growth. Critics say the model lacks empirical support, and Branko Milanović notes that bringing everyone to rich countries' median income would require world GDP to triple. Economists continue to dispute it.

openers.growth-theory-and-the-environment: How do economies grow, and how do populations? This chapter sets the two side by side. Population growth is simply the increase in the number of people, and logistic models show it slowing as it nears the carrying capacity, the largest population an environment can sustain. Economists explain long-run growth with the Solow–Swan model, built on saving, more workers and technological progress. Its later versions add education, and its leftover, the part of growth nothing else explains, has become a measure of productivity itself.
openers.growth-decoupling-and-limits: Can the economy keep growing on a planet with finite resources? A 1972 report, The Limits to Growth, simulated the question and warned of overshoot. Since then the debate has split into camps: some trust decoupling, growth without a matching rise in pressure on the environment, and call for green growth. Others warn that efficiency backfires through the rebound effect, or argue for degrowth, a planned, democratic reduction of production and consumption. Between them sit new pictures of a good economy, such as the doughnut, which joins planetary limits with a floor of basic human needs.

reviews.growth-theory-and-the-environment: Growth theory and population science share a shape. A population following a logistic path slows as it nears carrying capacity, and in the {{ref:nature-eecon-204}} capital meets diminishing returns, so growth from saving alone fades away. Only technological progress, measured by the {{ref:nature-eecon-205}}, keeps income per person rising. Later models added human capital to explain why poor countries fall behind, and the AK model dropped diminishing returns altogether. None of them includes nature's limits, which is the gap the next chapter takes up.
